{"answer": "# Part (a): Particle Size and Shape from 2D Backlit Images (Static Image Analysis)

## Systematic Differences Between SIA, Laser Diffraction, and Sieving

Static image analysis (SIA, ISO 13322-1) and laser diffraction (LD, ISO 13320) measure fundamentally different equivalent diameters, leading to systematic differences in d10, d50, and d90 that depend on particle shape, the image-analysis diameter definition, and the weighting basis. SIA typically determines an area-equivalent circular diameter (ECAD) or a Feret diameter from 2D projections, initially on a number basis, whereas LD infers a volume-weighted equivalent-sphere diameter from scattering patterns (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000003).

For non-spherical pharmaceutical particles, Tinke et al. reported that SIA-ECAD gave substantially higher d10 and d50 than LD but similar or lower d90, thereby narrowing the apparent PSD. For example, in Compound B SIA-ECAD yielded d10/d50/d90 of 9.7/17.0/27.7 µm versus 5.7/14.1/36.4 µm for LD—d10 was 70% higher, d50 21% higher, but d90 was 24% lower (pqac-00000057, pqac-00000001). Similar trends held for Compounds C and D, with SIA d10 29–73% higher and d50 34–39% higher than LD (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000057). Barreiros et al. found that microscopy d50 was approximately 13% higher than Malvern LD for irregular crushed glass (70.30 vs 62.04 µm) and approximately 24% higher for mica (79.05 vs 63.86 µm), with the ordering d50(SediGraph) < d50(Coulter) < d50(Malvern) < d50(Microscope) (pqac-00000006).

The following table summarizes the key comparative data:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

For sieving (ASTM B214/B822), the measured diameter corresponds to the minimum cross-section that passes a mesh opening, which differs from both the area-equivalent and scattering-equivalent diameters. Sieving and LD typically agree better for near-spherical powders but diverge for elongated or plate-like particles (pqac-00000003).

## Number-to-Volume Conversion

SIA intrinsically produces a number-weighted distribution, since each detected particle contributes one count. Converting to a volume-weighted distribution requires cubing each particle's measured diameter (assuming sphericity), which dramatically increases the influence of a small number of large particles while suppressing the contribution of many small particles (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004). The conversion shifts d50 and d90 upward and can substantially change the distribution shape, especially for broad or skewed PSDs. A quantitative example illustrates the effect: measuring 500 particles microscopically, of which 5% (∼25 particles) exceed 20 µm, yields an RSD of approximately 20% for that fraction in the number basis and approximately 14% when expressed as the corresponding ∼70% volume fraction (pqac-00000000). The conversion also amplifies any error in measuring the largest particles, making d90 inherently less precise than d50 in image-derived volume distributions (pqac-00000006).

## Number of Particles Needed for a Given Precision

The minimum particle count depends strongly on distribution polydispersity. Wouters et al. (2025), using electron microscopy of nanomaterials with subsampling strategies, reported optimal particle counts (Nopt) for Fmin (analogous to d50): 136 particles for a low-polydispersity material (ERM-FD100), 189 for medium polydispersity (TiO₂RM), and 513 for high polydispersity (BaSO₄RM). For d90, the corresponding Nopt values were 193, 261, and 575 particles, respectively, yielding total expanded uncertainties of approximately 11–14% (pqac-00000022). At lower precision targets, low-polydispersity materials (IQR% ≤ 30) need only 35 particles for 10% uncertainty in the median, while highly polydisperse materials (IQR% 55–80) require approximately 260 particles for the same uncertainty and approximately 1000 particles for 5% uncertainty (pqac-00000024). General literature recommendations for SIA range from 100 to 14,000 particles depending on the application, with 10,000 particles yielding approximately 1% RSD for d50 (pqac-00000025).

## Dispersion of Cohesive Fine Powders on Slides

Dispersing cohesive powders onto slides is critical for unbiased SIA. ISO 13322-1 recommends dispersing in an inert medium to prevent agglomeration. Wet dispersion—suspending powder in a suitable solvent with surfactant, then depositing a thin film on a glass slide—is generally preferred for cohesive fine powders because it separates primary particles more effectively than dry spreading (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000062). For dry dispersion, instruments such as the Sympatec RODOS use high-velocity air to deagglomerate and disperse powder onto a measurement surface (pqac-00000059). The interlaboratory characterization study by Linsinger et al. for non-spherical corundum reference materials showed within-laboratory standard deviations of 3.9–7.5% and between-laboratory standard deviations of 9–24% for SIA, with sample preparation (including dispersion) identified as a major contributor to the larger uncertainty (pqac-00000064). Particles below approximately 3 µm are problematic for optical SIA because diffraction halos cause substantial size overestimation and inaccurate shape measurement (pqac-00000023).

## Resolution Limits (Pixels per Particle)

The smallest particle of interest should occupy at least 5–10 pixels across its diameter for reliable size measurement by SIA (pqac-00000023). The theoretical diffraction-limited detection limit of optical microscopy is approximately 0.2 µm, but particles below approximately 0.8 µm are often not imageable under realistic conditions, and the practical lower limit for quantitative measurement is approximately 3 µm (pqac-00000023). For the user's Raspberry Pi HQ camera with a 0.12–1.8× zoom lens, the 12.3 MP sensor (4056 × 3040 pixels, 1.55 µm pixel pitch) at 1.8× magnification would give an image pixel size of approximately 0.86 µm/pixel, theoretically resolving particles down to approximately 4–9 µm (5–10 pixels) if optical quality is sufficient. At the typical AM powder range of 15–45 µm, particles would span 17–52 pixels, well above the minimum.

## Low-Cost Camera/Smartphone Microscopes

Several low-cost microscopy platforms have been validated against reference instruments, though primarily for airborne particulate matter and biological samples rather than bulk powder PSD. Wu et al. demonstrated a smartphone-based lens-free microscopy platform (c-Air) with approximately 93% particle sizing accuracy for PM₂.₅/PM₁₀, validated against EPA-approved beta-attenuation monitors (pqac-00000023). Zhang et al. developed an ultra-low-cost (<$4 USD) smartphone microscope with approximately 5 µm focus-tuning accuracy, using CycleGAN image enhancement to approach benchtop microscope quality (pqac-00000023). However, no published study was identified that directly validates a Raspberry Pi or smartphone camera-based SIA system against laser diffraction or sieving for bulk powder PSD (d10/d50/d90) in the AM-relevant size range. This represents an open gap that the user's planned work could fill.

---

# Part (b): Laboratory Powder Spreading Rigs for Powder-Bed AM

## Spreadability Metrics

No standardized spreadability metric has yet been established (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000029). The metrics used across published laboratory spreading rigs include:

- **Coverage**: Build-plate coverage percentage, empty-patch frequency, size, and area (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000032)
- **Packing fraction / layer density**: Mass of spread layer divided by layer volume, or expressed as a fraction of solid, tapped, or apparent density. Hulme et al. proposed ≥40% of apparent density as a screening threshold (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000043)
- **Areal mass / deposition rate**: Mass per unit area or mass deposited per unit time (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000012)
- **Surface roughness**: Ra, RMS roughness from profilometry or laser scanning (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000009)
- **Uniformity indicators**: Brightness variation, convex hull, bounding box from imaging (pqac-00000028)
- **Coordination number**: From DEM simulations (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000008)

Streaks have not been formalized as a named metric but are implicitly captured through roughness, empty-patch, and uniformity measurements.

The following table summarizes the major spreading rigs and their findings:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

## Effect of Gap (Layer Thickness) and Speed

**Gap thickness** (expressed in particle diameters) has a strong positive effect on spreading quality. DEM simulations by Fouda and Bayly using idealized Ti-6Al-4V particles showed that packing fraction increases almost linearly with gap thickness across gaps of 2–6 particle diameters (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000021). Increasing gap size also reduces the frequency and size of empty patches and decreases jamming probability (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000013). At a gap of 4d and 100 mm/s, Fouda and Bayly reported a packing fraction of 35% immediately behind the blade, falling to 25.8% in the final deposited layer due to residual particle inertia (pqac-00000055).

**Spreading speed** generally degrades layer quality. Shaheen et al. reported blade-spread mass fractions (MF) of approximately 50% at 10 mm/s, dropping to 20–30% at 50 mm/s and approximately 20% at 100 mm/s. A counter-clockwise rotating roller achieved a maximum MF of approximately 60% at 10 mm/s, consistently outperforming the blade (pqac-00000051). Higher speeds increase surface roughness, porosity, and particle collision effects, reduce coordination number, and promote looser packing (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011).

## Repeatability

Hulme et al. reported that their thin-film applicator test was repeatable and reproducible: for Powder G spread at 150 µm nominal thickness and 150 mm/s, two independent operators obtained mean layer densities of 3.89 ± 0.26 and 4.02 ± 0.51 g/cm³, with both measurements within one standard deviation of each other (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000048). Manual spreading rigs showed poorer repeatability due to operator-dependent positioning and velocity errors (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000033).

## Flowability Metrics as Predictors of Spreadability

The literature consistently finds that flowability and spreadability are related but distinct properties, and that traditional flowability metrics do not reliably predict spreading quality individually:

- **Angle of repose (AOR)**: High AOR is qualitatively associated with poor spreading (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015), and Carr categories can indicate general flow regime, but no universal quantitative correlation with spreading packing fraction has been established (pqac-00000039).
- **Hausner ratio (HR)**: Listed among flowability assessments and qualitatively associated with better spreading at lower values, but no direct HR-to-spreadability quantitative correlation was established (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041).
- **Rotating drum avalanche angle**: Considered more representative of spreading dynamics than static AOR because it incorporates dynamic powder behavior (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000038). Brocksieper et al. found conditional correlations between drum and rheometer metrics and spreading roughness, but these depended on recoater type and speed (pqac-00000038).
- **Shear-cell ffc**: Classifies powders from very cohesive (ffc < 2) to free flowing (ffc > 10) but was not found to reliably predict spreading performance; shear-cell testing may fail to detect some flowability changes relevant to spreading (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000042).
- **Hall flow**: Did not correlate with spread layer density in Hulme et al.'s 24-powder study, though the two powders that failed to spread also failed the Hall funnel (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000043).
- **FT4 specific energy**: Higher specific energy (greater interparticle friction) was linked to poorer deposition and lower final-part quality in stainless steel, making it a more promising candidate metric than traditional ones (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041).

## DEM Validation of Spreading Rigs

DEM validation for powder spreading typically involves calibrating contact parameters (friction, cohesion, restitution) using independent experiments—commonly angle of repose, powder heap profile, or packing density—and then comparing simulated layer properties against experimental measurements (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000016). Avrampos and Vosniakos validated their DEM model by cross-checking simulated angle of repose and angle of avalanche against experiments. Lampitella et al. validated DEM parameters through ad hoc experiments and simulated two spreading velocities representing different flow regimes (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000056). The key limitation is that many DEM studies use idealized spherical, monodisperse, non-cohesive particles, which may not represent real polydisperse AM powder behavior (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000050).

## Numbers for AlSi10Mg, 316L, and Ti-6Al-4V

- **Ti-6Al-4V**: Fouda and Bayly's DEM study used idealized spherical Ti-6Al-4V particles and obtained a final layer packing fraction of 25.8% at gap = 4d and blade speed = 100 mm/s (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000021). Brika and Brailovski tested gas-atomized Ti-6Al-4V (d10 = 25.3, d50 = 35.8, d90 = 46.4 µm) in their instrumented apparatus across 30–100 µm layers and 100–500 mm/s speeds. In Hulme et al., Ti-6Al-4V powder J (d50 = 34 µm, apparent density 2.52 g/cm³) was tested and successfully formed thin layers (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000027).
- **AlSi10Mg**: Hulme et al. tested AlSi10Mg powder K (d50 = 38 µm, 25–45 µm fraction, apparent density 1.34 g/cm³, mean aspect ratio 0.93) (pqac-00000045). AlSi10Mg was found to be especially sensitive to moisture: its rougher, more irregular morphology made flowability and spread-layer relative density more humidity-dependent than Ti-6Al-4V or Inconel 718, though air drying improved its spreading performance (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000034).
- **316L stainless steel**: Multiple 316L powders spanning nominal fractions from 0–20 to 90–150 µm were tested in Hulme et al., with apparent densities ranging from approximately 3.01 to 4.33 g/cm³ (pqac-00000045). {"answer": "# Part (a): Particle Size and Shape from 2D Backlit Images (Static Image Analysis)

## Systematic Differences Between SIA, Laser Diffraction, and Sieving

Static image analysis (SIA, ISO 13322-1) and laser diffraction (LD, ISO 13320) measure fundamentally different equivalent diameters, leading to systematic differences in d10, d50, and d90 that depend on particle shape, the image-analysis diameter definition, and the weighting basis. SIA typically determines an area-equivalent circular diameter (ECAD) or a Feret diameter from 2D projections, initially on a number basis, whereas LD infers a volume-weighted equivalent-sphere diameter from scattering patterns (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000003).

For non-spherical pharmaceutical particles, Tinke et al. reported that SIA-ECAD gave substantially higher d10 and d50 than LD but similar or lower d90, thereby narrowing the apparent PSD. For example, in Compound B SIA-ECAD yielded d10/d50/d90 of 9.7/17.0/27.7 µm versus 5.7/14.1/36.4 µm for LD—d10 was 70% higher, d50 21% higher, but d90 was 24% lower (pqac-00000057, pqac-00000001). Similar trends held for Compounds C and D, with SIA d10 29–73% higher and d50 34–39% higher than LD (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000057). Barreiros et al. found that microscopy d50 was approximately 13% higher than Malvern LD for irregular crushed glass (70.30 vs 62.04 µm) and approximately 24% higher for mica (79.05 vs 63.86 µm), with the ordering d50(SediGraph) < d50(Coulter) < d50(Malvern) < d50(Microscope) (pqac-00000006).

The following table summarizes the key comparative data:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

For sieving (ASTM B214/B822), the measured diameter corresponds to the minimum cross-section that passes a mesh opening, which differs from both the area-equivalent and scattering-equivalent diameters. Sieving and LD typically agree better for near-spherical powders but diverge for elongated or plate-like particles (pqac-00000003).

## Number-to-Volume Conversion

SIA intrinsically produces a number-weighted distribution, since each detected particle contributes one count. Converting to a volume-weighted distribution requires cubing each particle's measured diameter (assuming sphericity), which dramatically increases the influence of a small number of large particles while suppressing the contribution of many small particles (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004). The conversion shifts d50 and d90 upward and can substantially change the distribution shape, especially for broad or skewed PSDs. A quantitative example illustrates the effect: measuring 500 particles microscopically, of which 5% (∼25 particles) exceed 20 µm, yields an RSD of approximately 20% for that fraction in the number basis and approximately 14% when expressed as the corresponding ∼70% volume fraction (pqac-00000000). The conversion also amplifies any error in measuring the largest particles, making d90 inherently less precise than d50 in image-derived volume distributions (pqac-00000006).

## Number of Particles Needed for a Given Precision

The minimum particle count depends strongly on distribution polydispersity. Wouters et al. (2025), using electron microscopy of nanomaterials with subsampling strategies, reported optimal particle counts (Nopt) for Fmin (analogous to d50): 136 particles for a low-polydispersity material (ERM-FD100), 189 for medium polydispersity (TiO₂RM), and 513 for high polydispersity (BaSO₄RM). For d90, the corresponding Nopt values were 193, 261, and 575 particles, respectively, yielding total expanded uncertainties of approximately 11–14% (pqac-00000022). At lower precision targets, low-polydispersity materials (IQR% ≤ 30) need only 35 particles for 10% uncertainty in the median, while highly polydisperse materials (IQR% 55–80) require approximately 260 particles for the same uncertainty and approximately 1000 particles for 5% uncertainty (pqac-00000024). General literature recommendations for SIA range from 100 to 14,000 particles depending on the application, with 10,000 particles yielding approximately 1% RSD for d50 (pqac-00000025).

## Dispersion of Cohesive Fine Powders on Slides

Dispersing cohesive powders onto slides is critical for unbiased SIA. ISO 13322-1 recommends dispersing in an inert medium to prevent agglomeration. Wet dispersion—suspending powder in a suitable solvent with surfactant, then depositing a thin film on a glass slide—is generally preferred for cohesive fine powders because it separates primary particles more effectively than dry spreading (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000062). For dry dispersion, instruments such as the Sympatec RODOS use high-velocity air to deagglomerate and disperse powder onto a measurement surface (pqac-00000059). The interlaboratory characterization study by Linsinger et al. for non-spherical corundum reference materials showed within-laboratory standard deviations of 3.9–7.5% and between-laboratory standard deviations of 9–24% for SIA, with sample preparation (including dispersion) identified as a major contributor to the larger uncertainty (pqac-00000064). Particles below approximately 3 µm are problematic for optical SIA because diffraction halos cause substantial size overestimation and inaccurate shape measurement (pqac-00000023).

## Resolution Limits (Pixels per Particle)

The smallest particle of interest should occupy at least 5–10 pixels across its diameter for reliable size measurement by SIA (pqac-00000023). The theoretical diffraction-limited detection limit of optical microscopy is approximately 0.2 µm, but particles below approximately 0.8 µm are often not imageable under realistic conditions, and the practical lower limit for quantitative measurement is approximately 3 µm (pqac-00000023). For the user's Raspberry Pi HQ camera with a 0.12–1.8× zoom lens, the 12.3 MP sensor (4056 × 3040 pixels, 1.55 µm pixel pitch) at 1.8× magnification would give an image pixel size of approximately 0.86 µm/pixel, theoretically resolving particles down to approximately 4–9 µm (5–10 pixels) if optical quality is sufficient. At the typical AM powder range of 15–45 µm, particles would span 17–52 pixels, well above the minimum.

## Low-Cost Camera/Smartphone Microscopes

Several low-cost microscopy platforms have been validated against reference instruments, though primarily for airborne particulate matter and biological samples rather than bulk powder PSD. Wu et al. demonstrated a smartphone-based lens-free microscopy platform (c-Air) with approximately 93% particle sizing accuracy for PM₂.₅/PM₁₀, validated against EPA-approved beta-attenuation monitors (pqac-00000023). Zhang et al. developed an ultra-low-cost (<$4 USD) smartphone microscope with approximately 5 µm focus-tuning accuracy, using CycleGAN image enhancement to approach benchtop microscope quality (pqac-00000023). However, no published study was identified that directly validates a Raspberry Pi or smartphone camera-based SIA system against laser diffraction or sieving for bulk powder PSD (d10/d50/d90) in the AM-relevant size range. This represents an open gap that the user's planned work could fill.

---

# Part (b): Laboratory Powder Spreading Rigs for Powder-Bed AM

## Spreadability Metrics

No standardized spreadability metric has yet been established (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000029). The metrics used across published laboratory spreading rigs include:

- **Coverage**: Build-plate coverage percentage, empty-patch frequency, size, and area (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000032)
- **Packing fraction / layer density**: Mass of spread layer divided by layer volume, or expressed as a fraction of solid, tapped, or apparent density. Hulme et al. proposed ≥40% of apparent density as a screening threshold (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000043)
- **Areal mass / deposition rate**: Mass per unit area or mass deposited per unit time (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000012)
- **Surface roughness**: Ra, RMS roughness from profilometry or laser scanning (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000009)
- **Uniformity indicators**: Brightness variation, convex hull, bounding box from imaging (pqac-00000028)
- **Coordination number**: From DEM simulations (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000008)

Streaks have not been formalized as a named metric but are implicitly captured through roughness, empty-patch, and uniformity measurements.

The following table summarizes the major spreading rigs and their findings:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

## Effect of Gap (Layer Thickness) and Speed

**Gap thickness** (expressed in particle diameters) has a strong positive effect on spreading quality. DEM simulations by Fouda and Bayly using idealized Ti-6Al-4V particles showed that packing fraction increases almost linearly with gap thickness across gaps of 2–6 particle diameters (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000021). Increasing gap size also reduces the frequency and size of empty patches and decreases jamming probability (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000013). At a gap of 4d and 100 mm/s, Fouda and Bayly reported a packing fraction of 35% immediately behind the blade, falling to 25.8% in the final deposited layer due to residual particle inertia (pqac-00000055).

**Spreading speed** generally degrades layer quality. Shaheen et al. reported blade-spread mass fractions (MF) of approximately 50% at 10 mm/s, dropping to 20–30% at 50 mm/s and approximately 20% at 100 mm/s. A counter-clockwise rotating roller achieved a maximum MF of approximately 60% at 10 mm/s, consistently outperforming the blade (pqac-00000051). Higher speeds increase surface roughness, porosity, and particle collision effects, reduce coordination number, and promote looser packing (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011).

## Repeatability

Hulme et al. reported that their thin-film applicator test was repeatable and reproducible: for Powder G spread at 150 µm nominal thickness and 150 mm/s, two independent operators obtained mean layer densities of 3.89 ± 0.26 and 4.02 ± 0.51 g/cm³, with both measurements within one standard deviation of each other (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000048). Manual spreading rigs showed poorer repeatability due to operator-dependent positioning and velocity errors (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000033).

## Flowability Metrics as Predictors of Spreadability

The literature consistently finds that flowability and spreadability are related but distinct properties, and that traditional flowability metrics do not reliably predict spreading quality individually:

- **Angle of repose (AOR)**: High AOR is qualitatively associated with poor spreading (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015), and Carr categories can indicate general flow regime, but no universal quantitative correlation with spreading packing fraction has been established (pqac-00000039).
- **Hausner ratio (HR)**: Listed among flowability assessments and qualitatively associated with better spreading at lower values, but no direct HR-to-spreadability quantitative correlation was established (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041).
- **Rotating drum avalanche angle**: Considered more representative of spreading dynamics than static AOR because it incorporates dynamic powder behavior (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000038). Brocksieper et al. found conditional correlations between drum and rheometer metrics and spreading roughness, but these depended on recoater type and speed (pqac-00000038).
- **Shear-cell ffc**: Classifies powders from very cohesive (ffc < 2) to free flowing (ffc > 10) but was not found to reliably predict spreading performance; shear-cell testing may fail to detect some flowability changes relevant to spreading (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000042).
- **Hall flow**: Did not correlate with spread layer density in Hulme et al.'s 24-powder study, though the two powders that failed to spread also failed the Hall funnel (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000043).
- **FT4 specific energy**: Higher specific energy (greater interparticle friction) was linked to poorer deposition and lower final-part quality in stainless steel, making it a more promising candidate metric than traditional ones (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041).

## DEM Validation of Spreading Rigs

DEM validation for powder spreading typically involves calibrating contact parameters (friction, cohesion, restitution) using independent experiments—commonly angle of repose, powder heap profile, or packing density—and then comparing simulated layer properties against experimental measurements (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000016). Avrampos and Vosniakos validated their DEM model by cross-checking simulated angle of repose and angle of avalanche against experiments. Lampitella et al. validated DEM parameters through ad hoc experiments and simulated two spreading velocities representing different flow regimes (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000056). The key limitation is that many DEM studies use idealized spherical, monodisperse, non-cohesive particles, which may not represent real polydisperse AM powder behavior (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000050).

## Numbers for AlSi10Mg, 316L, and Ti-6Al-4V

- **Ti-6Al-4V**: Fouda and Bayly's DEM study used idealized spherical Ti-6Al-4V particles and obtained a final layer packing fraction of 25.8% at gap = 4d and blade speed = 100 mm/s (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000021). Brika and Brailovski tested gas-atomized Ti-6Al-4V (d10 = 25.3, d50 = 35.8, d90 = 46.4 µm) in their instrumented apparatus across 30–100 µm layers and 100–500 mm/s speeds. In Hulme et al., Ti-6Al-4V powder J (d50 = 34 µm, apparent density 2.52 g/cm³) was tested and successfully formed thin layers (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000027).
- **AlSi10Mg**: Hulme et al. tested AlSi10Mg powder K (d50 = 38 µm, 25–45 µm fraction, apparent density 1.34 g/cm³, mean aspect ratio 0.93) (pqac-00000045). - **316L stainless steel**: Multiple 316L powders spanning nominal fractions from 0–20 to 90–150 µm were tested in Hulme et al., with apparent densities ranging from approximately 3.01 to 4.33 g/cm³ (pqac-00000045). In counter-rolling DEM by Chen et al. (reported in Haydari), 316L packing density decreased and roughness increased as spreading speed increased (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000049). Hulme et al. proposed that 316L powders of similar size showed similar spreading performance, with one exception (Powder N performing notably better than same-sized peers) (pqac-00000043).

Overall, the literature supports that laboratory spreading rigs using thin-film applicators or modular testbeds can reproducibly rank powders, but no single traditional flowability metric (AOR, HR, avalanche angle, ffc) independently predicts spreading quality, and DEM validation for specific alloys remains largely qualitative rather than quantitatively validated against alloy-specific experimental data."}

state.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A 25 mm OD tube with a 21 mm bore and a helical flight ends in a 3 mm outlet; a NEMA 11 stepper turns it at 1-109 rpm, servos tilt it 0-90 degrees, a solenoid taps it, and doses fall onto a 0.1 mg analytical balance. We record a dosing fingerprint (mass per revolution vs tilt and speed, mass per tap, afterflow, no-flow fraction) on 13 powders (NaCl, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg, silicon, rice flours, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 dihydrate, fumed silica and others) and calibrate a LIGGGHTS DEM twin. Property labels from handbooks limit our models (angle-of-repose ranges 6-16 degrees wide), so we are designing ten small in-house tests built around the doser, each using a few grams and run on the same jar and day as the fingerprint: (1) heap angle of repose on a 20 mm fixed pedestal on the balance, photographed in silhouette; (2) bulk and tapped density in a 10 mL Class A cylinder filled by the auger and tapped by a cam drop of 3 mm at 250 taps/min, column height read by camera; (3) a servo tilting plate with an IMU: wall friction of a 25 mm powder-filled ring at 70-450 Pa on PLA, stainless steel and glass, and the start angle of 1-5 mm powder layers; (4) particle size and shape from backlit images with a Raspberry Pi HQ camera and a 0.12-1.8x zoom lens; (5) a 25 mm cup with 1-6 mm orifice discs and a servo gate emptying onto the balance (Beverloo fit, smallest orifice that flows, with and without taps); (6) humidity chambers held by saturated salt solutions (MgCl2, Mg(NO3)2, NaCl, KCl, silica gel) with SHT45 sensors, weighing uptake and dosing before and after; (7) a 40 mm by 15 mm rotating drum driven by the doser's stepper, 1-20 rpm; (8) unconfined yield strength of a 20 mm by 40 mm column from a split mould after 0.2-2 kPa consolidation, crushed by a lead-screw platen on a 100 g load cell; (9) a blade spreading a 0.1-0.2 mm layer over a 100 x 30 mm coupon at 10-100 mm/s; (10) a Faraday cup (aluminium cup in a grounded can) with a femtoamp op-amp charge amplifier under the doser outlet. Sieving and LD typically agree better for near-spherical powders but diverge for elongated or plate-like particles (hogg2008issuesinparticle pages 4-5).

## Number-to-Volume Conversion

SIA intrinsically produces a number-weighted distribution, since each detected particle contributes one count. Converting to a volume-weighted distribution requires cubing each particle's measured diameter (assuming sphericity), which dramatically increases the influence of a small number of large particles while suppressing the contribution of many small particles (merkus2018particlesandnanoparticles pages 22-24, hogg2008issuesinparticle pages 4-5, merkus2018particlesandnanoparticles pages 19-22). The conversion shifts d50 and d90 upward and can substantially change the distribution shape, especially for broad or skewed PSDs. A quantitative example illustrates the effect: measuring 500 particles microscopically, of which 5% (∼25 particles) exceed 20 µm, yields an RSD of approximately 20% for that fraction in the number basis and approximately 14% when expressed as the corresponding ∼70% volume fraction (merkus2018particlesandnanoparticles pages 22-24). The conversion also amplifies any error in measuring the largest particles, making d90 inherently less precise than d50 in image-derived volume distributions (barreiros1996calculatingshapefactors pages 3-4).

## Number of Particles Needed for a Given Precision

The minimum particle count depends strongly on distribution polydispersity. Wouters et al. (2025), using electron microscopy of nanomaterials with subsampling strategies, reported optimal particle counts (Nopt) for Fmin (analogous to d50): 136 particles for a low-polydispersity material (ERM-FD100), 189 for medium polydispersity (TiO₂RM), and 513 for high polydispersity (BaSO₄RM). For d90, the corresponding Nopt values were 193, 261, and 575 particles, respectively, yielding total expanded uncertainties of approximately 11–14% (wouters2025assessingparticlecount pages 7-9). At lower precision targets, low-polydispersity materials (IQR% ≤ 30) need only 35 particles for 10% uncertainty in the median, while highly polydisperse materials (IQR% 55–80) require approximately 260 particles for the same uncertainty and approximately 1000 particles for 5% uncertainty (wouters2025assessingparticlecount pages 6-7). General literature recommendations for SIA range from 100 to 14,000 particles depending on the application, with 10,000 particles yielding approximately 1% RSD for d50 (schnepf2023apracticalprimer pages 4-5).

## Dispersion of Cohesive Fine Powders on Slides

Dispersing cohesive powders onto slides is critical for unbiased SIA. ISO 13322-1 recommends dispersing in an inert medium to prevent agglomeration. Wet dispersion—suspending powder in a suitable solvent with surfactant, then depositing a thin film on a glass slide—is generally preferred for cohesive fine powders because it separates primary particles more effectively than dry spreading (merkus2018particlesandnanoparticles pages 19-22, linsinger2019preparationandcharacterisation pages 10-13). For dry dispersion, instruments such as the Sympatec RODOS use high-velocity air to deagglomerate and disperse powder onto a measurement surface (linsinger2019preparationandcharacterisation pages 1-6). The interlaboratory characterization study by Linsinger et al. for non-spherical corundum reference materials showed within-laboratory standard deviations of 3.9–7.5% and between-laboratory standard deviations of 9–24% for SIA, with sample preparation (including dispersion) identified as a major contributor to the larger uncertainty (linsinger2019preparationandcharacterisation pages 13-17). Particles below approximately 3 µm are problematic for optical SIA because diffraction halos cause substantial size overestimation and inaccurate shape measurement (schnepf2023apracticalprimer pages 5-7).

## Resolution Limits (Pixels per Particle)

The smallest particle of interest should occupy at least 5–10 pixels across its diameter for reliable size measurement by SIA (schnepf2023apracticalprimer pages 5-7). The theoretical diffraction-limited detection limit of optical microscopy is approximately 0.2 µm, but particles below approximately 0.8 µm are often not imageable under realistic conditions, and the practical lower limit for quantitative measurement is approximately 3 µm (schnepf2023apracticalprimer pages 5-7). For the user's Raspberry Pi HQ camera with a 0.12–1.8× zoom lens, the 12.3 MP sensor (4056 × 3040 pixels, 1.55 µm pixel pitch) at 1.8× magnification would give an image pixel size of approximately 0.86 µm/pixel, theoretically resolving particles down to approximately 4–9 µm (5–10 pixels) if optical quality is sufficient. At the typical AM powder range of 15–45 µm, particles would span 17–52 pixels, well above the minimum.

## Low-Cost Camera/Smartphone Microscopes

Several low-cost microscopy platforms have been validated against reference instruments, though primarily for airborne particulate matter and biological samples rather than bulk powder PSD. Wu et al. demonstrated a smartphone-based lens-free microscopy platform (c-Air) with approximately 93% particle sizing accuracy for PM₂.₅/PM₁₀, validated against EPA-approved beta-attenuation monitors (schnepf2023apracticalprimer pages 5-7). Zhang et al. developed an ultra-low-cost (<$4 USD) smartphone microscope with approximately 5 µm focus-tuning accuracy, using CycleGAN image enhancement to approach benchtop microscope quality (schnepf2023apracticalprimer pages 5-7). However, no published study was identified that directly validates a Raspberry Pi or smartphone camera-based SIA system against laser diffraction or sieving for bulk powder PSD (d10/d50/d90) in the AM-relevant size range. This represents an open gap that the user's planned work could fill.

# Part (b): Laboratory Powder Spreading Rigs for Powder-Bed AM

## Spreadability Metrics

No standardized spreadability metric has yet been established (hulme2023apracticableand pages 1-2, talebi2021characterisationofspreadabilityb pages 46-49). The metrics used across published laboratory spreading rigs include:

- **Coverage**: Build-plate coverage percentage, empty-patch frequency, size, and area (haydari2021thespreadingbehaviourb pages 48-51, haydari2021thespreadingbehavioura pages 48-51, haydari2021thespreadingbehaviourd pages 48-51)
- **Packing fraction / layer density**: Mass of spread layer divided by layer volume, or expressed as a fraction of solid, tapped, or apparent density. Hulme et al. proposed ≥40% of apparent density as a screening threshold (hulme2023apracticableand pages 1-2, hulme2023apracticableand pages 10-11)
- **Areal mass / deposition rate**: Mass per unit area or mass deposited per unit time (haydari2021thespreadingbehaviour pages 51-54, haydari2021thespreadingbehaviourb pages 48-51)
- **Surface roughness**: Ra, RMS roughness from profilometry or laser scanning (brocksieper2026investigationofflowability pages 1-2, haydari2021thespreadingbehaviour pages 51-54)
- **Uniformity indicators**: Brightness variation, convex hull, bounding box from imaging (whiting2023powderspreadingtestbed pages 9-12)
- **Coordination number**: From DEM simulations (haydari2021thespreadingbehaviour pages 51-54, talebi2021characterisationofspreadabilitya pages 40-43)

Streaks have not been formalized as a named metric but are implicitly captured through roughness, empty-patch, and uniformity measurements.

## Effect of Gap (Layer Thickness) and Speed

**Gap thickness** (expressed in particle diameters) has a strong positive effect on spreading quality. DEM simulations by Fouda and Bayly using idealized Ti-6Al-4V particles showed that packing fraction increases almost linearly with gap thickness across gaps of 2–6 particle diameters (fouda2019ademstudy pages 11-12, fouda2019ademstudy pages 1-2). Increasing gap size also reduces the frequency and size of empty patches and decreases jamming probability (haydari2021thespreadingbehaviour pages 51-54, haydari2021thespreadingbehavioura pages 48-51). At a gap of 4d and 100 mm/s, Fouda and Bayly reported a packing fraction of 35% immediately behind the blade, falling to 25.8% in the final deposited layer due to residual particle inertia (fouda2019ademstudy pages 11-12).

**Spreading speed** generally degrades layer quality. Shaheen et al. reported blade-spread mass fractions (MF) of approximately 50% at 10 mm/s, dropping to 20–30% at 50 mm/s and approximately 20% at 100 mm/s. A counter-clockwise rotating roller achieved a maximum MF of approximately 60% at 10 mm/s, consistently outperforming the blade (shaheen2021theinfluenceof pages 9-12). Higher speeds increase surface roughness, porosity, and particle collision effects, reduce coordination number, and promote looser packing (haydari2021thespreadingbehaviour pages 51-54, haydari2021thespreadingbehavioura pages 51-54, haydari2021thespreadingbehaviourb pages 51-54).

## Repeatability

Hulme et al. reported that their thin-film applicator test was repeatable and reproducible: for Powder G spread at 150 µm nominal thickness and 150 mm/s, two independent operators obtained mean layer densities of 3.89 ± 0.26 and 4.02 ± 0.51 g/cm³, with both measurements within one standard deviation of each other (hulme2023apracticableand pages 8-10, hulme2023apracticableand pages 4-5). Manual spreading rigs showed poorer repeatability due to operator-dependent positioning and velocity errors (talebi2021characterisationofspreadabilityb pages 46-49, talebi2021characterisationofspreadabilitya pages 46-49).

## Flowability Metrics as Predictors of Spreadability

The literature consistently finds that flowability and spreadability are related but distinct properties, and that traditional flowability metrics do not reliably predict spreading quality individually:

- **Angle of repose (AOR)**: High AOR is qualitatively associated with poor spreading (talebi2021characterisationofspreadabilitya pages 46-49, talebi2021characterisationofspreadability pages 46-49), and Carr categories can indicate general flow regime, but no universal quantitative correlation with spreading packing fraction has been established (haydari2021thespreadingbehaviour pages 27-31).
- **Hausner ratio (HR)**: Listed among flowability assessments and qualitatively associated with better spreading at lower values, but no direct HR-to-spreadability quantitative correlation was established (haydari2021thespreadingbehavioura pages 31-34, haydari2021thespreadingbehaviour pages 31-34, haydari2021thespreadingbehaviourb pages 31-34).
- **Rotating drum avalanche angle**: Considered more representative of spreading dynamics than static AOR because it incorporates dynamic powder behavior (haydari2021thespreadingbehavioura pages 31-34, haydari2021thespreadingbehaviourc pages 31-34, brocksieper2026investigationofflowability pages 1-2). Brocksieper et al. found conditional correlations between drum and rheometer metrics and spreading roughness, but these depended on recoater type and speed (brocksieper2026investigationofflowability pages 1-2).
- **Shear-cell ffc**: Classifies powders from very cohesive (ffc < 2) to free flowing (ffc > 10) but was not found to reliably predict spreading performance; shear-cell testing may fail to detect some flowability changes relevant to spreading (haydari2021thespreadingbehaviour pages 27-31, haydari2021thespreadingbehaviourc pages 27-31).
- **Hall flow**: Did not correlate with spread layer density in Hulme et al.'s 24-powder study, though the two powders that failed to spread also failed the Hall funnel (hulme2023apracticableand pages 1-2, hulme2023apracticableand pages 10-11).
- **FT4 specific energy**: Higher specific energy (greater interparticle friction) was linked to poorer deposition and lower final-part quality in stainless steel, making it a more promising candidate metric than traditional ones (haydari2021thespreadingbehavioura pages 31-34, haydari2021thespreadingbehaviour pages 31-34, haydari2021thespreadingbehaviourb pages 31-34).

## DEM Validation of Spreading Rigs

DEM validation for powder spreading typically involves calibrating contact parameters (friction, cohesion, restitution) using independent experiments—commonly angle of repose, powder heap profile, or packing density—and then comparing simulated layer properties against experimental measurements (lampitella2021discreteelementmethod pages 1-2, haydari2021thespreadingbehavioura pages 51-54). Avrampos and Vosniakos validated their DEM model by cross-checking simulated angle of repose and angle of avalanche against experiments. Lampitella et al. validated DEM parameters through ad hoc experiments and simulated two spreading velocities representing different flow regimes (lampitella2021discreteelementmethod pages 1-2, lampitella2021discreteelementmethod pages 9-11). The key limitation is that many DEM studies use idealized spherical, monodisperse, non-cohesive particles, which may not represent real polydisperse AM powder behavior (haydari2021thespreadingbehavioura pages 51-54).

## Numbers for AlSi10Mg, 316L, and Ti-6Al-4V

- **Ti-6Al-4V**: Fouda and Bayly's DEM study used idealized spherical Ti-6Al-4V particles and obtained a final layer packing fraction of 25.8% at gap = 4d and blade speed = 100 mm/s (fouda2019ademstudy pages 11-12, fouda2019ademstudy pages 1-2). Brika and Brailovski tested gas-atomized Ti-6Al-4V (d10 = 25.3, d50 = 35.8, d90 = 46.4 µm) in their instrumented apparatus across 30–100 µm layers and 100–500 mm/s speeds. In Hulme et al., Ti-6Al-4V powder J (d50 = 34 µm, apparent density 2.52 g/cm³) was tested and successfully formed thin layers (hulme2023apracticableand pages 2-4).
- **AlSi10Mg**: Hulme et al. tested AlSi10Mg powder K (d50 = 38 µm, 25–45 µm fraction, apparent density 1.34 g/cm³, mean aspect ratio 0.93) (hulme2023apracticableand pages 2-4). AlSi10Mg was found to be especially sensitive to moisture: its rougher, more irregular morphology made flowability and spread-layer relative density more humidity-dependent than Ti-6Al-4V or Inconel 718, though air drying improved its spreading performance (haydari2021thespreadingbehaviourd pages 48-51, haydari2021thespreadingbehaviourc pages 48-51).
- **316L stainless steel**: Multiple 316L powders spanning nominal fractions from 0–20 to 90–150 µm were tested in Hulme et al., with apparent densities ranging from approximately 3.01 to 4.33 g/cm³ (hulme2023apracticableand pages 2-4). In counter-rolling DEM by Chen et al. (reported in Haydari), 316L packing density decreased and roughness increased as spreading speed increased (haydari2021thespreadingbehavioura pages 51-54, haydari2021thespreadingbehaviourc pages 51-54). Hulme et al. proposed that 316L powders of similar size showed similar spreading performance, with one exception (Powder N performing notably better than same-sized peers) (hulme2023apracticableand pages 10-11).

Overall, the literature supports that laboratory spreading rigs using thin-film applicators or modular testbeds can reproducibly rank powders, but no single traditional flowability metric (AOR, HR, avalanche angle, ffc) independently predicts spreading quality, and DEM validation for specific alloys remains largely qualitative rather than quantitatively validated against alloy-specific experimental data.

For d90, the corresponding Nopt values were 193, 261, and 575 particles, respectively, yielding total expanded uncertainties of approximately 11–14% (pqac-00000022). At lower precision targets, low-polydispersity materials (IQR% ≤ 30) need only 35 particles for 10% uncertainty in the median, while highly polydisperse materials (IQR% 55–80) require approximately 260 particles for the same uncertainty and approximately 1000 particles for 5% uncertainty (pqac-00000024). General literature recommendations for SIA range from 100 to 14,000 particles depending on the application, with 10,000 particles yielding approximately 1% RSD for d50 (pqac-00000025).

## Dispersion of Cohesive Fine Powders on Slides

Dispersing cohesive powders onto slides is critical for unbiased SIA. ISO 13322-1 recommends dispersing in an inert medium to prevent agglomeration. Wet dispersion—suspending powder in a suitable solvent with surfactant, then depositing a thin film on a glass slide—is generally preferred for cohesive fine powders because it separates primary particles more effectively than dry spreading (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000062). For dry dispersion, instruments such as the Sympatec RODOS use high-velocity air to deagglomerate and disperse powder onto a measurement surface (pqac-00000059). The interlaboratory characterization study by Linsinger et al. for non-spherical corundum reference materials showed within-laboratory standard deviations of 3.9–7.5% and between-laboratory standard deviations of 9–24% for SIA, with sample preparation (including dispersion) identified as a major contributor to the larger uncertainty (pqac-00000064). Particles below approximately 3 µm are problematic for optical SIA because diffraction halos cause substantial size overestimation and inaccurate shape measurement (pqac-00000023).

## Resolution Limits (Pixels per Particle)

The smallest particle of interest should occupy at least 5–10 pixels across its diameter for reliable size measurement by SIA (pqac-00000023). The theoretical diffraction-limited detection limit of optical microscopy is approximately 0.2 µm, but particles below approximately 0.8 µm are often not imageable under realistic conditions, and the practical lower limit for quantitative measurement is approximately 3 µm (pqac-00000023). For the user's Raspberry Pi HQ camera with a 0.12–1.8× zoom lens, the 12.3 MP sensor (4056 × 3040 pixels, 1.55 µm pixel pitch) at 1.8× magnification would give an image pixel size of approximately 0.86 µm/pixel, theoretically resolving particles down to approximately 4–9 µm (5–10 pixels) if optical quality is sufficient. At the typical AM powder range of 15–45 µm, particles would span 17–52 pixels, well above the minimum.

## Low-Cost Camera/Smartphone Microscopes

Several low-cost microscopy platforms have been validated against reference instruments, though primarily for airborne particulate matter and biological samples rather than bulk powder PSD. Wu et al. demonstrated a smartphone-based lens-free microscopy platform (c-Air) with approximately 93% particle sizing accuracy for PM₂.₅/PM₁₀, validated against EPA-approved beta-attenuation monitors (pqac-00000023). Zhang et al. developed an ultra-low-cost (<$4 USD) smartphone microscope with approximately 5 µm focus-tuning accuracy, using CycleGAN image enhancement to approach benchtop microscope quality (pqac-00000023). However, no published study was identified that directly validates a Raspberry Pi or smartphone camera-based SIA system against laser diffraction or sieving for bulk powder PSD (d10/d50/d90) in the AM-relevant size range. This represents an open gap that the user's planned work could fill.

# Part (b): Laboratory Powder Spreading Rigs for Powder-Bed AM

## Spreadability Metrics

No standardized spreadability metric has yet been established (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000029). The metrics used across published laboratory spreading rigs include:

- **Coverage**: Build-plate coverage percentage, empty-patch frequency, size, and area (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000032)
- **Packing fraction / layer density**: Mass of spread layer divided by layer volume, or expressed as a fraction of solid, tapped, or apparent density. Hulme et al. proposed ≥40% of apparent density as a screening threshold (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000043)
- **Areal mass / deposition rate**: Mass per unit area or mass deposited per unit time (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000012)
- **Surface roughness**: Ra, RMS roughness from profilometry or laser scanning (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000009)
- **Uniformity indicators**: Brightness variation, convex hull, bounding box from imaging (pqac-00000028)
- **Coordination number**: From DEM simulations (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000008)

Streaks have not been formalized as a named metric but are implicitly captured through roughness, empty-patch, and uniformity measurements.

## Effect of Gap (Layer Thickness) and Speed

**Gap thickness** (expressed in particle diameters) has a strong positive effect on spreading quality. DEM simulations by Fouda and Bayly using idealized Ti-6Al-4V particles showed that packing fraction increases almost linearly with gap thickness across gaps of 2–6 particle diameters (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000021). Increasing gap size also reduces the frequency and size of empty patches and decreases jamming probability (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000013). At a gap of 4d and 100 mm/s, Fouda and Bayly reported a packing fraction of 35% immediately behind the blade, falling to 25.8% in the final deposited layer due to residual particle inertia (pqac-00000055).

**Spreading speed** generally degrades layer quality. Shaheen et al. reported blade-spread mass fractions (MF) of approximately 50% at 10 mm/s, dropping to 20–30% at 50 mm/s and approximately 20% at 100 mm/s. A counter-clockwise rotating roller achieved a maximum MF of approximately 60% at 10 mm/s, consistently outperforming the blade (pqac-00000051). Higher speeds increase surface roughness, porosity, and particle collision effects, reduce coordination number, and promote looser packing (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011).

## Repeatability

Hulme et al. reported that their thin-film applicator test was repeatable and reproducible: for Powder G spread at 150 µm nominal thickness and 150 mm/s, two independent operators obtained mean layer densities of 3.89 ± 0.26 and 4.02 ± 0.51 g/cm³, with both measurements within one standard deviation of each other (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000048). Manual spreading rigs showed poorer repeatability due to operator-dependent positioning and velocity errors (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000033).

## Flowability Metrics as Predictors of Spreadability

The literature consistently finds that flowability and spreadability are related but distinct properties, and that traditional flowability metrics do not reliably predict spreading quality individually:

- **Angle of repose (AOR)**: High AOR is qualitatively associated with poor spreading (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015), and Carr categories can indicate general flow regime, but no universal quantitative correlation with spreading packing fraction has been established (pqac-00000039).
- **Hausner ratio (HR)**: Listed among flowability assessments and qualitatively associated with better spreading at lower values, but no direct HR-to-spreadability quantitative correlation was established (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041).
- **Rotating drum avalanche angle**: Considered more representative of spreading dynamics than static AOR because it incorporates dynamic powder behavior (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000038). Brocksieper et al. found conditional correlations between drum and rheometer metrics and spreading roughness, but these depended on recoater type and speed (pqac-00000038).
- **Shear-cell ffc**: Classifies powders from very cohesive (ffc < 2) to free flowing (ffc > 10) but was not found to reliably predict spreading performance; shear-cell testing may fail to detect some flowability changes relevant to spreading (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000042).
- **Hall flow**: Did not correlate with spread layer density in Hulme et al.'s 24-powder study, though the two powders that failed to spread also failed the Hall funnel (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000043).
- **FT4 specific energy**: Higher specific energy (greater interparticle friction) was linked to poorer deposition and lower final-part quality in stainless steel, making it a more promising candidate metric than traditional ones (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041).

## DEM Validation of Spreading Rigs

DEM validation for powder spreading typically involves calibrating contact parameters (friction, cohesion, restitution) using independent experiments—commonly angle of repose, powder heap profile, or packing density—and then comparing simulated layer properties against experimental measurements (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000016). Avrampos and Vosniakos validated their DEM model by cross-checking simulated angle of repose and angle of avalanche against experiments. Lampitella et al. validated DEM parameters through ad hoc experiments and simulated two spreading velocities representing different flow regimes (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000056). The key limitation is that many DEM studies use idealized spherical, monodisperse, non-cohesive particles, which may not represent real polydisperse AM powder behavior (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000050).

## Numbers for AlSi10Mg, 316L, and Ti-6Al-4V

- **Ti-6Al-4V**: Fouda and Bayly's DEM study used idealized spherical Ti-6Al-4V particles and obtained a final layer packing fraction of 25.8% at gap = 4d and blade speed = 100 mm/s (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000021). Brika and Brailovski tested gas-atomized Ti-6Al-4V (d10 = 25.3, d50 = 35.8, d90 = 46.4 µm) in their instrumented apparatus across 30–100 µm layers and 100–500 mm/s speeds. In Hulme et al., Ti-6Al-4V powder J (d50 = 34 µm, apparent density 2.52 g/cm³) was tested and successfully formed thin layers (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000027).
- **AlSi10Mg**: Hulme et al. tested AlSi10Mg powder K (d50 = 38 µm, 25–45 µm fraction, apparent density 1.34 g/cm³, mean aspect ratio 0.93) (pqac-00000045). AlSi10Mg was found to be especially sensitive to moisture: its rougher, more irregular morphology made flowability and spread-layer relative density more humidity-dependent than Ti-6Al-4V or Inconel 718, though air drying improved its spreading performance (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000034).
- **316L stainless steel**: Multiple 316L powders spanning nominal fractions from 0–20 to 90–150 µm were tested in Hulme et al., with apparent densities ranging from approximately 3.01 to 4.33 g/cm³ (pqac-00000045). In counter-rolling DEM by Chen et al. (reported in Haydari), 316L packing density decreased and roughness increased as spreading speed increased (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000049). Hulme et al. proposed that 316L powders of similar size showed similar spreading performance, with one exception (Powder N performing notably better than same-sized peers) (pqac-00000043).

Overall, the literature supports that laboratory spreading rigs using thin-film applicators or modular testbeds can reproducibly rank powders, but no single traditional flowability metric (AOR, HR, avalanche angle, ffc) independently predicts spreading quality, and DEM validation for specific alloys remains largely qualitative rather than quantitatively validated against alloy-specific experimental data.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that static image analysis (SIA) and laser diffraction (LD) can produce systematically different particle-size distributions for nonspherical, especially rectangular, particles. SIA directly measures two-dimensional particle dimensions by optical microscopy, whereas LD measures a scattering pattern and processes it using an assumption of spherical particles. For rectangular particles, LD is dominated by projected area and scattering intensity rather than by a single geometric particle size. A particle with length L and breadth B is approximately represented by diffraction diameters corresponding to L and B, but differences in scattering intensity cause the LD volume distribution to weight contributions approximately as A²/L and A²/B. Consequently, LD may overestimate the shortest dimension and underestimate the longest dimension relative to image-derived dimensions, with particle orientation and orientation averaging further broadening the reported distribution. It also contains no sample-size calculations or recommendations for how many particles are required to achieve a specified precision for d50 or d90. The method generally assumes spherical particles and reports an equivalent spherical size based on particle volume. Consequently, nonspherical particles such as needles and platelets can lead to reduced accuracy, because their two-dimensional shape features are not represented adequately by a single equivalent sphere. The excerpt also notes that multiple particles scattering light simultaneously can make calculations inaccurate, so particle concentration must be controlled. For particles below the laser wavelength, Mie theory requires the real and imaginary refractive indices; uncertainty in the imaginary component can substantially affect results, including a reported example of 50% variation in d10. Differences in detector arrangement and algorithms among laser-diffraction instruments can also cause variability when measuring the same powder. The supplied pages do not discuss number-to-volume conversion explicitly or provide particle-count/precision formulas.

It states that particle size is generally reported as an equivalent-sphere diameter, and that irregularly shaped particles can produce substantially different diameter measurements depending on the definition and measurement method. Different techniques may therefore yield different results for the same powder, particularly because their algorithms convert particle shape effects into an equivalent spherical response differently. contexts.context: The excerpt identifies powder-layer quality using coverage or uniformity, packing fraction/density, solid volume fraction, surface roughness, bulk density, coordination number, deposition or mass-flow rate, and the frequency of empty patches (a manifestation of jamming). It does not specifically report areal mass or streaks, although deposition rate and mass flow rate are discussed. Increasing gap thickness generally improves spreading: empty-patch frequency decreases, total volume and mass flow increase, and packing fraction, packing density, and coordination number rise, eventually reaching a stable value. In the DEM study, gap sizes of 2–6 particle diameters produced a linear increase in packing fraction. However, excessively large gaps can compromise dimensional accuracy. Increasing spreading/rake speed generally worsens layer quality: packing fraction and density decrease, while surface roughness increases; higher speed also promotes dragging, lower coordination, and looser powder beds. Speed can increase deposition rate and avalanche-angle change, but mass flow eventually becomes asymptotic. The cited passage only gives a qualitative angle-of-repose relationship: steel spreaders perform better for powders with low angles of repose, whereas silicone performs better for powders with lower flowability. No direct correlations are provided here for Hausner ratio or shear-cell ffc.

These include mass or areal amount of deposited powder, spreading throughput, porosity, packing fraction or packing density, coordination number, surface roughness, surface uniformity, and the occurrence or size of empty patches. Experimental spreading was performed using a manually operated rake with an exchangeable blade whose height could be adjusted above a flat aluminum build platform. Powder-bed density was measured using additively manufactured cylinders: unmelted powder was removed from the cylinder interior, its mass was recorded, and the empty volume was determined by backfilling the cylinder with water. Dividing powder mass by powder volume yielded bed density; dividing this value by the solid IN718 density yielded relative packing density, and porosity was calculated as one minus relative packing density. The DEM model represented spreading direction, build direction, particle size distribution, gravity-driven powder deposition, and a rectangular spreader, while spreader elastic deformation was neglected. It explains that the required number of measured particles depends on the particle collective, its size and shape distributions, polydispersity, agglomeration, subsampling effects, and the desired precision. General recommendations cited in the article range from 100 to 14,000 particles for size measurement. As an example of precision, measuring 10,000 microplastics is reported to yield a relative standard deviation of 1% for particle size. Broader particle-size distributions require measuring a larger proportion of the bulk, particularly to characterize the sparsely populated upper tail. The article recommends determining the minimum number individually for each particle collective; possible approaches include monitoring stabilization of the mean or standard deviation, or using a chi-square goodness-of-fit test. Thus, this excerpt supports only general sample-size guidance and indicates that a precise d50/d90-specific number would need to be obtained from the cited references or other sections of the article. contexts.context: The excerpt discusses image analysis as an individual-particle method in which particles are examined one at a time and their sizes are determined by direct measurement. It notes that individual-particle counting methods are particularly susceptible to detection limits, and that imaging systems can address limited size range by using progressively higher magnification. Combining measurements from different magnifications requires matching separate data sets, which can introduce substantial errors for broad particle-size distributions. Table 2 gives sample-size requirements for determining a powder size distribution with less than 5% relative error under specified assumptions: particle density of 2.5 g/cm3 and 1% by weight in the top-size fraction. The listed required sample sizes are 200 kg for a 1 cm maximum particle size, 200 g for 1 mm, 0.2 g for 100 μm, 0.2 mg for 10 μm, and 0.2 μg for 1 μm. However, this excerpt does not provide a particle-count formula specifically for precision in d50 or d90, nor does it state a minimum number of pixels per particle or a numerical resolution limit for static image analysis.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide specific particle-count formulas or numerical sample sizes for achieving a given precision of d50 and d90. It gives a general rule of thumb: measure at least 300 environmental microplastics and 10,000 milled microplastics, while noting that the appropriate number depends on the statistical property being controlled and should ideally be established using prior studies or a pilot study. For reliable particle-size measurement, the smallest particle of interest should occupy at least five to ten pixels in the image; this generally requires sufficiently high magnification. Regarding resolution limits for static light-microscope image analysis, the theoretical detection limit is 0.2 µm, but particles below approximately 0.8 µm are often not imageable under realistic conditions. In practice, particles smaller than 3 µm are discouraged because diffraction halos cause substantial size overestimation and inaccurate shape measurement. Thus, the practical resolution limit is approximately 3 µm for reliable measurement, despite lower theoretical and conditional imaging limits.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a laboratory spreadability rig intended to provide a simple, inexpensive, semi-automated alternative to manual spreading, X-ray imaging, 3D scanning, and other more specialized methods. It uses a TQC Sheen AB4120 Automatic Film Applicator, a custom-machined 316L steel base plate, and Elcometer 3560/1 and 3560/2 gap applicators. Adhesive tape restricts the spread width to 50 mm, while interchangeable applicator edges generate nominal layer thicknesses of approximately 80, 110, 140, or 170 µm for the 3560/1 and 100, 150, … µm for the 3560/2. Powder is weighed before spreading, and the plate includes a through-thickness opening to collect excess powder; the stated objective is to calculate powder density in the thin layer. The table reports powder properties rather than measured spread-layer densities or areal masses. For Ti-6Al-4V (Powder J), nominal bulk density is 4.43 g/cm³ and apparent density is 2.52 g/cm³. AlSi10Mg (K) has values of 2.66 and 1.34 g/cm³, respectively. The listed 316L powders have nominal bulk density of 8.03 g/cm³ and apparent densities ranging roughly from 3.01 to 4.33 g/cm³. This excerpt does not provide packing fractions, spread-layer areal mass, or quantitative repeatability results.

contexts.context: This excerpt describes a laboratory spreadability test for metal additive-manufacturing powders. A single powder layer is spread with commercial equipment originating from the paint and food industries, and the resulting layer density is measured. The study evaluates density relative to each powder’s apparent density rather than reporting areal mass or packing fraction as separate metrics in the supplied text. Twenty-four powders from eight suppliers were examined; 22 successfully formed thin layers, achieving at least 40% of their respective apparent densities. Measured layer density was sensitive to the spreading-plate roughness, recoater speed, nominal layer thickness, particle size, and particle aspect ratio. The authors characterize the procedure as repeatable and reproducible, but the excerpt provides no numerical repeatability statistics, such as standard deviations, coefficients of variation, or repeatability limits. It also does not give alloy-specific layer-density, areal-mass, or packing-fraction values for AlSi10Mg, 316L stainless steel, or Ti-6Al-4V. The test was benchmarked against the Hall flowmeter, but Hall flow time did not correlate with spread-layer density; notably, the two powders that failed to spread also failed to pass through the Hall funnel. The excerpt therefore supports general test-rig and metric information, but not detailed alloy-specific quantitative results.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that powder spreadability in PBF-LB/M can correlate with conventional flowability measurements, but the relationships are conditional rather than universal. Prior work cited in the introduction found correlations between powder application quality and the angle of repose, as well as the dynamic angle (avalanche angle) measured in a rotating drum. Other cited studies reported that rotating-drum and powder-rheometer metrics corresponded to observed spreading behavior, and the present study established connections between spreadability and flowability parameters from a powder rheometer and rotating drum. However, the excerpt does not provide specific results for the Hausner ratio or shear-cell flow function (ffc), so it cannot establish whether either metric predicts spreading quality. More broadly, the authors emphasize that the combined effects of powder properties, recoater type, and recoating speed remain incompletely understood. The study used global powder-bed surface roughness, measured with a laser scanner, as a suitable spreadability evaluation parameter. Recoater conditions matter substantially: the roller produced the lowest roughness across powder types and speeds, suggesting that traditional flowability metrics alone are unlikely to reliably predict spreading quality independently of the application system and process parameters.

A 25 cm³ starting powder volume was selected, exceeding twice the maximum envisaged 9.8 cm³ layer volume. Results indicated that increasing recoater speed decreased measured density, while base-plate roughness affected density differently for thin and thick layers. Two powders, identified only as H and X, showed extremely low spreadability; the other powders had similar performance. contexts.context: The excerpt discusses DEM and related simulations of powder spreading, but it does not report specific numerical packing-fraction or packing-density values for Ti-6Al-4V, 316L, or other powders. The reported findings are qualitative. Xiang et al. found that increasing bed height or gap size increases packing density and coordination number, while compression also increases both quantities and counterbalances the effect of layer thickness. Mono-sized powders were reported to improve packing density and coordination number. Fouda et al., using spherical mono-sized non-cohesive particles and a vertical blade, found that the deposited-layer packing fraction is lower than that of the initial powder heap because of shear-induced dilation, dilation while passing through the gap, and post-blade inertial motion. Their results indicate that larger gap sizes and lower blade velocities increase packing fraction. The study also cautions that mono-sized spherical particles may produce packing fractions that do not represent real AM powder batches. Meier et al. reported lower packing fraction and poorer surface uniformity with decreasing particle size and increasing cohesiveness, while greater nominal layer thickness improved layer quality. For counter-rolling 316L powder, Chen et al. found that increasing spreading speed decreases layer packing density and coordination number while increasing surface roughness, producing a looser layer. Other cited simulations assess packing fraction or volume fraction, but no numerical values are provided in this excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports spread-layer mass fraction (MF), used as the layer packing-density metric, for DEM simulations with blade and counter-clockwise rotating-roller spreaders. Across the investigated parameter space, the rotating roller achieved a maximum MF of approximately 60%, whereas the blade achieved approximately 50%. contexts.context: The excerpt describes two certified reference materials, ERM-FD066 and ERM-FD069, developed for particle-size-distribution measurements of non-spherical, polydisperse materials. For static image analysis, the certified measurand is the number-weighted area-equivalent circular diameter determined according to ISO 13322-1, with microscope calibration providing traceability to the SI metre. For laser diffraction, the certified measurand is based on percentiles of the volume-weighted equivalent spherical diameter obtained according to ISO 13320. ERM-FD066 was characterised using both wet and dry dispersion and Mie theory with a refractive index of 1.77 + 0i; ERM-FD069 was characterised using Mie theory and the Fraunhofer approximation, with differences between wet and dry dispersion included in the uncertainty. The materials were judged suitable for quality control: laser-diffraction expanded uncertainties were 1–4% for ERM-FD069 and 3–9% for ERM-FD066, while image-analysis uncertainties were larger but still suitable for quality control. The supplied excerpt does not report the numerical systematic differences in d10, d50, and d90 between static image analysis and laser diffraction. It only emphasizes that the two methods quantify differently defined measurands, so their percentile values are not necessarily directly equivalent.

contexts.context: Linsinger et al. reported two certified reference materials consisting of non-spherical, polydisperse corundum: ERM®-FD066 and ERM®-FD069. The materials were characterized for particle-size distribution using both static image analysis and laser diffraction. The excerpt indicates that laser-diffraction results showed very good agreement between instruments from different manufacturers, while static image analysis exhibited greater variation than is typically observed for spherical particles. However, the supplied pages contain a badly fragmented table/figure extraction. Although entries for x10,0, x50,0, x90,0 and corresponding laser-diffraction quantities are visible, the columns and material labels are not preserved sufficiently to establish the paired d10, d50, and d90 values or calculate reliable systematic differences between the two methods. Therefore, this excerpt supports identification of the CRMs and the general method-performance conclusions, but it does not provide an unambiguous numerical comparison of d10, d50, and d90. The original article’s intact tables or figures would be needed to report whether one method gave systematically higher or lower values and by how much.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies the two non-spherical, polydisperse certified reference materials as ERM-FD066 and ERM-FD069. ERM-FD066 is described as the smaller-particle material, while ERM-FD069 is the larger-particle material. Both were examined by optical microscopy/static image analysis and laser diffraction. For laser diffraction, the study assessed wet and dry dispersion and both Mie-theory and Fraunhofer evaluations. The excerpt does not provide the requested direct systematic differences in d10, d50, and d90 between static image analysis and laser diffraction, nor does it give paired method-specific values for those three percentiles. It does report systematic differences among laser-diffraction conditions: Mie versus Fraunhofer results differed by 20–80% at the lower percentiles for ERM-FD066, whereas differences for ERM-FD069 were only 1–4% above x5,3. Wet-versus-dry dispersion differences were 2.4–5.6% for ERM-FD066 using Mie theory and 0.7–4.2% for ERM-FD069. Thus, the excerpt supports identification of the CRMs and laser-method effects, but not a quantitative comparison of d10, d50, and d90 between imaging and laser diffraction.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A 25 mm OD tube with a 21 mm bore and a helical flight ends in a 3 mm outlet; a NEMA 11 stepper turns it at 1-109 rpm, servos tilt it 0-90 degrees, a solenoid taps it, and doses fall onto a 0.1 mg analytical balance. We record a dosing fingerprint (mass per revolution vs tilt and speed, mass per tap, afterflow, no-flow fraction) on 13 powders (NaCl, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg, silicon, rice flours, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 dihydrate, fumed silica and others) and calibrate a LIGGGHTS DEM twin. Property labels from handbooks limit our models (angle-of-repose ranges 6-16 degrees wide), so we are designing ten small in-house tests built around the doser, each using a few grams and run on the same jar and day as the fingerprint: (1) heap angle of repose on a 20 mm fixed pedestal on the balance, photographed in silhouette; (2) bulk and tapped density in a 10 mL Class A cylinder filled by the auger and tapped by a cam drop of 3 mm at 250 taps/min, column height read by camera; (3) a servo tilting plate with an IMU: wall friction of a 25 mm powder-filled ring at 70-450 Pa on PLA, stainless steel and glass, and the start angle of 1-5 mm powder layers; (4) particle size and shape from backlit images with a Raspberry Pi HQ camera and a 0.12-1.8x zoom lens; (5) a 25 mm cup with 1-6 mm orifice discs and a servo gate emptying onto the balance (Beverloo fit, smallest orifice that flows, with and without taps); (6) humidity chambers held by saturated salt solutions (MgCl2, Mg(NO3)2, NaCl, KCl, silica gel) with SHT45 sensors, weighing uptake and dosing before and after; (7) a 40 mm by 15 mm rotating drum driven by the doser's stepper, 1-20 rpm; (8) unconfined yield strength of a 20 mm by 40 mm column from a split mould after 0.2-2 kPa consolidation, crushed by a lead-screw platen on a 100 g load cell; (9) a blade spreading a 0.1-0.2 mm layer over a 100 x 30 mm coupon at 10-100 mm/s; (10) a Faraday cup (aluminium cup in a grounded can) with a femtoamp op-amp charge amplifier under the doser outlet.
